articles.headline: STOCKMEN Who Have Gathered Here To-Day Consider Well The Benefits of the Following Article And Act Accordingly.
articles.text:
Why not make this point the Territorial cattle headquarters? The opportunity is within your grasp, if you will only make an effort for it. We have here every natural and artifical advantage that could be asked. The cattle interests east of the Bad Lands are small and this point is virtually the farthest east and consequently the nearest to a market. The bulk of the cattle business of Western Dakota is on or tributary to the Little Missouri river. These two facts would alone be sufficient for establishing the Territorial headquarters here. But in addition we have the only railroad outlet for the cattle interests of Dakota. Beside these reasons the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co. furnishes a ready market for many cattle right at home. Any one of these facts would be sufficient to bring the headquarters here, but the four present an array of arguments that is unanswerable. Beyond all these facts no other place has made active efforts to be the headquarters. All seem naturally to look here as the best place. This meeting could easily organize as a Bad Lands association, pass all the legislation required, and then resolve itself into a preliminary meeting to issue a call for a Territorial convention to be held here on March 27, for instance. This will give sufficient time before the general round-up to let every one interested know of the project and also to pass any motions they may wish to have acted upon by the Montana association, which meets soon after. Many Montana, Wyoming and Colorado cattle men would undoubtedly join the association, and, then, what is to prevent this place becoming, in the course of time, the cattle center of the whole Northwest, with a huge association having its headquarters here. Both the above plans are reasonable and feasible. A very little effort will secure the first and time will be sure to bring the last.

THE COW BOY merely places these facts before the attention of the cattle men. It is for your and our own interests to take vigorous action upon them. Don't let this opportunity go by, but strike while the iron is hot and the prize is ours.
articles.summary: Editorial urging the stockmen meeting that day to organize a Bad Lands association and call a Territorial cattle convention at Little Missouri for March 27.

articles.text: We wish to say a word or two in reference to the Bad Lands as a sheep country. The report of the death of many of Marquis de Mores' sheep has been widely published and heralded abroad as an evidence of the unfitness of the Bad Lands for sheep raising. Let us examine the facts. The Marquis came here last May and in the fall, judging this to be a good sheep country, sent men east to buy a large herd. Right here we must mention that the whole thing was an experiment. No sheep had ever been raised here, there was no data to be governed by, and naturally there was a mistake made. The mistake in this instance was in buying merino sheep, shipping them here late in the fall, and providing no buildings for their protection. Any one of these reasons, viewed in the light of the experience of the last two months, would have been sufficient to make the project a failure. The total loss, however, has been greatly magnified. It is not at all likely that it will reach $5,000, and the experience gained is an ample return for the loss. On the other hand, look at some of the successful sheep raising in the Bad Lands. Howard Eaton has some of the large, long-wooled variety that also labored under the disadvantage of being driven upon new ranges late in the fall, but they have done as well as cattle. This winter has been a severe one on all kinds of stock, and the above amply proves that the Bad Lands is a sheep country, if the right kind of sheep are bred. Sheep cannot stand as much exposure as cattle and they need to get acquainted with the range earlier in the season. With protection from storms, and hay during the worst winter weather sheep will undoubtedly prove as remunerative in the Bad Lands as cattle. In the Red river valley, where the cold and exposure to storms are far greater than here, common Minnesota sheep do well. The same is true of Montana. Why, than, should not the Bad Lands, which has every natural advantage, make a better sheep country than either of them?
articles.summary: Editorial defending the Bad Lands as sheep country after widely reported losses among the Marquis de Morès' merino sheep, citing Howard Eaton's long-wooled flock.

articles.text: The cedar with which the Bad Lands abounds is the regular lead-pencil variety and makes excellent firewood. It is easily cut, close grained, burns readily and for a long time, and gives off an intense heat. In spite of the fact that coal is so plenty many here prefer to burn the cedar. If one has a team the cedar costs nothing beside the labor of cutting it.
articles.summary: Bad Lands cedar praised as firewood; many prefer it to the plentiful coal.

articles.text: Never was there a more delightful or welcome chinook than that of Sunday and Monday. As if by magic the grip of Boreas was broken and the snow begun disappearing from the buttes in roaring torrents of water. The ice of the Little Missouri river, three feet thick, was soon covered with two to three feet of water, and Tuesday, although it was again freezing, four feet of water. A sigh of relief has gone up from every cattle man in the Bad Lands. Now all possible danger is past. It is altogether likely that not a solitary head in the whole Bad Lands will die of exposure this winter or spring. This is the record that “the most God-forsaken country on earth, the tail-end of frozen-up Dakota,” publishes to the world. It speaks for itself.
articles.summary: A chinook on Sunday and Monday melted the snow and put up to four feet of water on the Little Missouri ice; cattlemen consider the winter danger past.

articles.text: One of the most sensible things done for a long time by a railroad is that of the Northern Pacific officials in concluding to lower emigrant rates. The difference in rates between the roads is almost the exclusive reason for the larger settlements in Southern Dakota. All those who have been in both sections readily appreciate the vast superiority of Northern Dakota. Up to this time, however, emigrants who had but little money have been almost compelled to go to Southern Dakota. We have never heard the right idea expressed better than by our genial Register at Bismarck, Mr. Rea. He says: “If I was running this thing I would conduct it like a church festival. Nothing to get in and five dollars to get out.”
articles.summary: The Northern Pacific has decided to lower emigrant rates, which the paper says will help settle northern Dakota; quotes Bismarck land-office Register Rea.

articles.text:
“The Deadwood merchants are determined to make the Northern Pacific route a freight route, as quite a number of them are ordering their stocks from the East via Dickinson. There is, however, an opinion among them that Dickinson will not long remain the point of transfer of goods from the cars to wagons, as Little Missouri station is much nearer the Hills.”

The above clipping from an article published in the Black Hills Journal gives a very good idea of the opinion of Deadwood merchants in respect to the relative merits of the Dickinson and Medora routes.
articles.summary: Black Hills Journal clipping: Deadwood merchants are shipping via the Northern Pacific and Dickinson but expect Little Missouri to become the transfer point.

articles.text: It is very seldom that an appointment is greeted with less opposition than was that of Judge Palmer to the vacancy on the bench caused by the death of Judge Kidder. There seems to be no doubt as to the eminent qualifications of Judge Palmer, but some of our exchanges would rather have had a Dakota man.
articles.summary: Comment on Judge Palmer's appointment to the Dakota bench vacancy left by Judge Kidder's death.

articles.headline: Black Leg.
articles.text: We hear of a few cases of black leg among calves on the range, though no one range reports more than half a dozen cases. Without going into a scientific discussion of the disease, or indulging in any big words, we want to say to ranchmen that there is very little trouble in getting rid of the plague. After the disease once takes hold of an animal it is all the same as a carcass, for it works rapidly. But the moment one of your calves dies with it, round all of the balance up and give them a sharp run for two or three miles and back, driving fast enough to get up an active circulation of the blood. Keep this up for a week and you will have no more black leg. No losses will occur from the time you commence this process. Should the disease break out again weeks later, repeat and keep it up until grass comes. It is sometimes difficult to get the calves together, but it is the only sure way of saving them that can be well resorted to on the open range.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped advice on treating black leg among range calves (credited to the N. W. Live Stock Journal), with a note of a few cases on the range.

articles.headline: Dakota as a Health Resort.
articles.text: At the regular annual meeting of the Chicago Academy of Homeopathic Physicians and Surgeons, a paper was read by Dr. T. C. Duncan on “Dakota as a Health Resort.” Premising that the essentials of a health resort are in its sources productive of diversion, deep respiration and vigorous digestion, the doctor showed that Dakota furnished such in a marked degree, the water, air and other favorable conditions contributing to the cure of dyspepsia, diseases of the kidneys and bladder, catarrh, bronchitis and consumption in its early stages, though in its advanced stages the patient should seek a warmer and less bracing air. Asthma is also markedly affected by Dakota air, which, moreover, is more beneficial than that of Colorado, or other elevated regions, in cases of heart disease, complicated by asthma, bronchitis or indigestion. The large amount of soda in the soil makes the wheat of Dakota especially healthful, while from its large amount of nitrogenous elements the use of this staple supplants the demand for meat.—[Chicago Daily news.
articles.summary: Clipped Chicago Daily News report of a paper by Dr. T. C. Duncan praising Dakota's climate as a health resort.

articles.text:
The friends of Mervine Thompson, the Cleveland slugger, are ready to back him for $25,000 against Sullivan. Thompson easily knocked out Stewart, champion of Canada, and Welch, champion of Pennsylvania. Sullivan was challenged some time ago by Ross, Thompson's backer, but nothing has been heard from the “culchahed” slugger.

A Russian noble recently lost $400,000 at cards in a single night at Paris. He lost the money at the Parisian club and it is thought he was cheated out of the amount as recent discoveries of marked cards have been made there, and some of the members have been incontinently “fired.”
articles.summary: Two short non-local news paragraphs: a prize-fight challenge to Sullivan and a Russian noble's card losses in Paris.

articles.headline: On the Range.
articles.text:
A total of 1,450 live cattle, [316?] live sheep, 10,566 quarters of dressed beef, 2,125 carcasses of mutton and 50 dressed pigs were exported from New York last week.—[Stockman.

The numerous inquiries for good stock ranches by men who are looking for locations in the new West would indicate an active business in all kinds of stock the coming season.—[Boomerang.

There is a perfect unanimity of opinion among all our exchanges relative to the condition of stock on the range. The report comes from all sides that cattle have never been in better condition at this season of the year.

Several subscribers ask for a remedy to keep lice off cattle. One ounce of crude carbolic acid mixed in one quart of water and applied warm is recommended as a sure cure. It also possesses healing properties—[Colorado Farmer.

Stock in this section is wintering splendidly, and we hear of no losses in the immediate neighborhood. We learn however, that parties on the Upper Poudre have lost considerably, the loss occurring entirely among herds that have recently been brought from the East.—[Loveland Leader.

The River Falls Cattle Company, whose range is on Powder river, will make a heavy shipment of stock cattle to this country early in the spring. Several members of the company are now in the East making purchases, and it is their intention to ship no less than 2,000 head.—[Miles City Press.

Parties in from Cherokee strip report cattle in good shape and well scattered out over the ranges. Plenty of good grass, water and appetites are taking the old sisters and families through in good shape. The boys would not give one per cent to have any one insure them ninety per cent of calves from their entire cow herds this spring.—[Caldwell Journal.

The grazing lands of Dakota, Montana, Colorado, Nebraska, Wyoming, Eastern Oregon and Idaho are estimated at 1,000,000,000 acres. The Northern Pacific railroad is now opening up a region capable of supporting 5,000,000 cattle and 10,000,000 sheep, which when it shall be fully occupied, can export yearly 600,000 cattle, 1,500,000 sheep and 10,000,000 pounds of wool.—[Northwest.

A Dallas, Tex., dispatch of the 7th says that information has been received here to the effect that George B. Loving, of this State, who is now in England representing the Texas Improvement Company, has sold a large amount of ranch property situated in four adjoining counties, on Double Mountain fork of the Brazos river, for $2,500,000. This is said to be the largest live stock transaction ever made.

It takes eleven pounds of milk to add one pound of live weight to a calf, and an ox that weighs 1,300 pounds will consume twenty-two pounds of hay in twenty-four hours to keep from losing weight. If he is to fatten he must have just twice that quanty, when he will gain two pounds a day. This is one pound live weight to eleven pounds of good hay. To obtain fifty cents a hundred for his hay a farmer must sell fat steers at $5.50 per hundred pounds.—]N. W. L. S. Journal.

We received a call last week from a young Mexican residing at Monclova, Miguel Arguindegui, who is interested in ranching in the state of Coahuila. He reports a good season and says stock are doing well. Speaking of selling cattle or other stock under estray laws, he says they are sold whenever it is found that the brand has not been recorded and no owner appears. At any time within six months the money may be reclaimed, but after that time it goes to the public. Brands should be recorded at the capital of a state, whence they will be forwarded to the different municipalities for general recording.—[Texas L. S. Journal.

The one thing our Northwestern cattle growers seem to be a “little off” in is the placing of strange cattle upon their ranges late in the season, so late that they do not become familiar with their surroundings until the winter is upon them. During the warm, pleasant days of the late spring and early summer animals will at once go to work on the inviting green sward, and very soon become as if to the manor born. But late in the season they have a disposition to wander in search of other and perhaps better ranges. They are restless and nervous, and do not take on fat preparatory for nature's trial season. In order to withstand the rigors of our northern climate, range animals need to be at home. Dumb animals have nerves and temperaments just as men have. They don't want any cheap “boarding house” experience. They want a regular home table, at which they are masters of ceremony. In order to acquire that contented feeling, they must be on the range in time to learn all the characteristics of their surroundings. Then they are contented and happy. Under such conditions will they take on fat and develop rapidly. If our herd owners would get all their cattle on the range by the middle of July each year the mortality of the range would be almost entirely overcome. Who ever heard of a native dying in this country from the vicissitudes of the climate? Of course, there is an occasional cow dies in the early spring from the effects of calf-dropping, but the bulk of the losses are confined to “rawhides,” or late arrivals.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Column of range and livestock items clipped from other papers (Stockman, Boomerang, Colorado Farmer, Loveland Leader, Miles City Press, Caldwell Journal, Northwest, Texas and N. W. Live Stock Journals).

articles.text: James Hannigan took in Bismarck and Mandan last week.
articles.summary: James Hannigan visited Bismarck and Mandan.

articles.text: George Smith made ye typo “smile” in the absence of the editor last week.
articles.summary: George Smith treated the printer while the editor was away.

articles.text: W. G. Hollins, one of Mandan's most prominent lawyers, was in town last week.
articles.summary: Mandan lawyer W. G. Hollins visited town.

articles.text: Jos. Pennell has gone to St. Paul to meet the Marquis and complete arrangements as to the freight route.
articles.summary: Joseph Pennell went to St. Paul to meet the Marquis de Morès about the freight route.

articles.text: Hayes Moore is in from the Killdeer mountains country where he has a first-rate ranch. He expects to stay but a short time.
articles.summary: Rancher Hayes Moore came in from the Killdeer Mountains.

articles.text: We will doubtless surprise our readers by the early appearance of THE COW BOY this morning, but a glance at our editorial page will disclose the reason.
articles.summary: The paper appeared early this morning; the editorial page explains why.

articles.text: The Tongue river bridge at Miles City was washed away by the flood of Sunday, and no passenger train came through from the west until yesterday morning.
articles.summary: The Sunday flood washed out the Tongue River bridge at Miles City, halting westbound-origin passenger trains until Wednesday.

articles.text: It is a magnificent sight to see the torrents of water rushing along on the ice of the Little Missouri river. When the ice breaks, however, the present spectacle will fade into insignificance.
articles.summary: Floodwater rushing over the Little Missouri ice.

articles.text: Messrs. Jones, of Deadwood; Meeks, of Sully, and Avery, of Augusta, Me., called during our absence. We regret not having seen the gentlemen and hope they will call again when we are “to hum.”
articles.summary: Visitors Jones of Deadwood, Meeks of Sully and Avery of Augusta, Me., called at the office.

articles.text: We made a trip to Bismarck and Mandan last Friday and Saturday and did not meet a person who had not read and liked THE COW BOY. Without a solitary solicitation on our part we received eleven cash subscribers.
articles.summary: The editor visited Bismarck and Mandan Friday and Saturday and gained eleven subscribers.

articles.text: Frank Smith, not to be outdone by his brother, yesterday brought in a petrifaction of a piece of cottonwood which seems to have petrified after the wood had dried and the veins separated slightly. It is a very curious specimen.
articles.summary: Frank Smith brought in a petrified cottonwood specimen.

articles.text: Messrs. Paddock and Roberts will soon do something for which the citizens will rise up and call them blessed. They propose to haul fifty or seventy-five loads of scoria and distribute it along the streets, thus forming a good road-bed even in the muddiest times.
articles.summary: Paddock and Roberts plan to surface the streets with scoria.

articles.text: Daniel Friedman started for Minnesota last Friday to buy cattle for Wm. Dantz. The latter will also start soon for the same purpose. They expect to buy 700 or 800 head, perhaps more. They return about April 1, and will drive the cattle to Mr. Dantz' present ranch.
articles.summary: Daniel Friedman left to buy 700-800 cattle in Minnesota for William Dantz.

articles.text: Subscriptions are coming in from places where we least expected them. From Minnesota especially we have received many subscriptions. A total stranger to us writes: “THE COW BOY suits me so well that you can count me as a subscriber until it gets to be an old man.”
articles.summary: Subscriptions arriving, especially from Minnesota.

articles.text: Lloyd Boberts started East last week to buy cattle. As we stated in a previous issue, Mr. Roberts is the pioneer cattle man of the Bad Lands. He has a good ranch about ten miles up the river and will stock it with first-rate cattle from Minnesota and Iowa. He will return in about a month.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts, called the pioneer cattleman of the Bad Lands, went East to buy cattle for his ranch ten miles up the river.

articles.text: E. G. Paddock has gone into partnership with Frank Moore to run the Pyramid Park Hotel. Many improvements will be made in the building, especially in the way of cutting up the second floor into rooms. The rush of tourists in the summer will undoubtedly repay the outlay abundantly.
articles.summary: E. G. Paddock joined Frank Moore in running the Pyramid Park Hotel, with improvements planned.

articles.text: Geo. Fitzgerald's wounded hand presents an appearance that a surgeon would call beautiful. Since the time of the accident the wound has not presented an unfavorable symptom and is now almost entirely healed. The action of the third finger may be enfeebled, but there is no danger of losing it.
articles.summary: George Fitzgerald's wounded hand is nearly healed.

articles.text: Stockmen readily appreciate the value of inserting their brands in THE COW BOY and several have come in lately. In the near future we will get new cuts much superior to those we now have and put our stockmen's brands on them without extra charge. It will be expensive, but as we will pay particular attention to this branch of advertising we propose to have the best.
articles.summary: The paper plans better brand cuts for stockmen's brand advertisements.

articles.text: Messrs. George Smith and Edwin Bulpin are the two latest contributors to our museum of Bad Lands curiosities. Mr. Smith donated two splendid specimens of scoria with a perfect impression of a leaf on each. Mr. Bulpin's gift was several fine specimens of gypsum and agate. Our collection seems to have awakened an active interest and although it will take a long time to obtain a complete collection its ultimate success is assured.
articles.summary: George Smith and Edwin Bulpin gave specimens to the paper's museum of Bad Lands curiosities.

articles.text: We will make a specialty of our “Sporting Notes” and in the same column will answer any question addressed to us on the subject. All questions that we cannot answer immediately we will get authority for before publishing the answer. We also make a specialty of records made in all sports and in the course of a season a careful perusal of our “Sporting Notes” will enable a reader of THE COW BOY to decide almost any question relative to sports.
articles.summary: The paper will answer readers' sporting questions in its Sporting Notes.

articles.text: The last report we heard about the men who stole the horses at Matthews' camp was that a posse had started in pursuit with every prospect of capturing them. It is very probable that if the thieves are caught it will occur to the captors that Mandan is altogether too far to take them for trial, and an impromptu necktie festival will be held. The Bad Lands has been wonderfully free from the depredations of horse thieves, and a dose of the above kind of medicine will tend to discourage any future attempts of the kind.
articles.summary: Horses were stolen at Matthews' camp and a posse was in pursuit; the paper predicts a lynching if they are caught.

articles.headline: OUR FREIGHT ROUTE. With a Big “OUR.”
articles.text:
Now that the matter is decided and only the final preliminaries to the opening remain to be settled concerning our freight route, things wear a rosy aspect that causes that “quiet smile to percolate about our features” in a manner wonderful to behold.

The gang of men that started out a week ago to-day, staked out the road to the level ridge east of the Little Missouri valley and found that there was only one place where the teams would have to be doubled. Grading will remedy this and after the ridge is reached, no difficulty at all is experienced clear to Deadwood. There is an abundance of wood and water and the route as a whole is a model one, better even than the old Bismarck-Deadwood route except for the few hills encountered before leaving the Bad Lands.

Mail stations have been picked out and the petitions have been forwarded to Washington. By this time probably, they have official sanction. They are three in number, the first at Grand river, Billings county; the second at Moreau, Harding county and the third at Belle, Butte county.

As we prophesied in our last issue, the route is now a question of a very short time. The trial trip will be made as soon as possible.
articles.summary: The Medora–Deadwood freight route is decided; a crew staked the road, three mail stations were proposed, and a trial trip is coming.

articles.text: Mr. Clark, of Little Falls, Minn., who has been with us several days has concluded to stay and make this his home. He will certainly find that he has used good judgment in coming to this decision and he will undoubtedly make us a valuable citizen.
articles.summary: Mr. Clark of Little Falls, Minn., decided to settle here.

articles.text:
To the land of the Dakotas,
To the region known as Bad Lands,
Came a festive lightning jerker,
“Which his name” was Edwin Bulpin.
Quick he was with ear and finger
To receive or send a message,
But his telegraphic learning
Helped him none in going hunting.
On the balmy day of Monday
When Chinook was softly blowing
Melting all the winter's snow-fall
Till the brooks were turned to rivers
And the creeks to mighty torrents,
Making mellow all the butte sides
By the death blow to the frost king,
Edwin started forth a hunting.
Tramped he with a stubborn purpose
Up and down the sloping coolies
On the buttes and in the canons
Till he saw a bird of omen
Of the Accipitres order
And the family Strigidae
In other words a common night owl,
Solemn-looking, blinking, staring,
Wishing for the we'come night-time
When it might pursue its booty.
Edwin saw it at distance
And he crept and crawled and wiggled
Till the muzzle of his rifle
Almost touched the owl's tail feathers.
Shut he both his optics closely!
Held his breath and pulled the trigger,
Then he looked at where the owl was,
Looked and wondered where he could be,
Till at last he thought that he had
Blown him out of all existence,
Stepped he forward to examine
And the treacherous butte-side yielded,
Giving way beneath the pressure
Of the No. 12's of Edwin.
Down he rolled with wild gyrations
To the bottom of the coolie.
Full two hundred lengthened paces
Was the depth where he had fallen
And the earth, soft with the melting,
Closed around him like a mantle,
Lying flat in this position
Edwin saw the bird of omen
Far above him on a cedar,
Thoughtful-looking and a wond'ring,
What the—skip it—was the matter.
articles.summary: Mock-Hiawatha verse about telegrapher Edwin Bulpin's owl hunt during Monday's chinook, ending with his tumble down a butte-side.

articles.text: We wish to call the especial attention of our readers to the advertisements of M. Kline and Mahar & Drury, of Mandan. Mr. Kline, by the excellence of his cigars has controlled that trade since his arrival at Mandan and he now proposes to put out a new and first-class brand, for sale exclusively at this point. We are expecting a box every day and our friends will then have a treat, as we never were known to use the naughty weed. Every one who has been in Mandan knows Tom Mahar and Ed Drury and will be pleased to know that the new firm is enjoying unbounded prosperity.
articles.summary: Puff for Mandan advertisers M. Kline (cigars) and Mahar & Drury.

articles.text: Messrs. Geo. Blankenberg and R. H. Montgomery, of Belfield, made Medora a visit Tuesday. They report good prospects for their town. Indeed, there is no reason why Belfield should not be one of the best towns in Western Dakota. It possesses many natural advantages and men of energy and capital are calling the attention of emigrants to it. What is Belfield's gain is our gain and we hope that it will be all its most sanguine friends wish.
articles.summary: George Blankenberg and R. H. Montgomery of Belfield visited Medora Tuesday.

articles.text: Since our first issue we have not seen an article in any of our exchanges relative to lawlessness in Little Missouri. We do not know whether our articles had the effect of stopping the scurrilous attacks or not. Certain it is they have ceased. The future of both Medora and Little Missouri is assured and the attacks referred to will soon be only a matter of remembrance.
articles.summary: Exchanges have stopped printing attacks on Little Missouri's lawlessness since the paper began.

articles.text: Messrs. Pennell & Roberts have kindly offered their large room over the “Senate” for the use of the stockmen for the meeting to-day. It is the only available room of sufficient size to be had. All reports from above show that a full meeting will be held, as every cow-man on the river takes a deep interest in the matters to be discussed.
articles.summary: The stockmen's meeting today will be held in Pennell & Roberts' room over the Senate.

articles.text: The Cœur D'Alene mines craze seems to have abated considerably. A man who has wintered here and will leave just as soon as the worst part of the season has passed and such bright prospects are constantly opening, should have a keeper appointed for him.
articles.summary: The Coeur d'Alene mining craze has abated locally.

articles.headline: Correspondence.
articles.text:
LITTLE MISSOURI, Feb. 27, 1884.

EDITOR COW BOY:

Another week is here, and more good things with it. Among them will be the coming meeting of the stockmen and the always welcome COW BOY.

Howard Eaton, must be frozen up and afraid that the visitors will be likewise afflicted, as he has chosen a place where hot water with some other stuff in it can be had.

We're informed that he is credited with the authorship of our last letter, but he hasn't any “savvey” as the Greasers say, about writing for a newspaper and is an innocent cuss in this matter. Frank Moore is also blamed, but the smarties are just as far off about him. “How” is a man who could just about fill Geary Paddock's clothes.

Many distinguished guests have come to the metropolis lately. Among them we noticed Charlie Mason, Nitche, Boland and other bloods.

Jack Bullion rides a good horse when he shows up in town.

Billy Paddock has come out as a hunter and guide since he quit cow punching. He intends to open an office and give all tourists the “proper steer” to the happy land. His last trip was with Weeks, of New York, and Hampton, of Columbia, S. C. Billy showed them the burning mine and then they rode down Custer's trail to Eaton's cow camp. Here the boys took in the eagle, wild geese, deer and buffalo, then came back here, and he kindly showed them how to oil their saddles so they wouldn't wear out the leather on a hunting trip of that kind.

A long man is apt to wear out a good saddle, especially if he has not ridden for a few months and is out of practice. Weeks and Hampton left here “very sore” but well pleased with their vist to this wonderful place. They hope to return in the hunting season.

Mose Ryder, with the gospel crew Moody and Sankey, is still up-river making his everlasting fortune. Nitche says that they had been very successful at the time he passed. They had only been at work four days and had almost one hundred posts cut. Senator Jones lends an airy dignity and respectabilty to the gang Mose says that he can't work as he used to do before he fell in the ditch near the railroad. He hurt his leg and caught “Jessie” generally.

If Steiger had been there a great contest would have occurred, as Mose wanted that claim sure.

Capt. Moore and John Nelson didn't tumble in time to join the gang, so had to climb up to the old garden.

It's tough on a Christain to read all we've written, but your patience is like Job's “biles,” slow to come to a head.

Some day we'll write again, until then

HOW.
articles.summary: Gossip letter signed “How”: Billy Paddock now guides tourists (Weeks of New York and Hampton of Columbia, S.C., hunted via the burning mine and Eaton's cow camp); Mose Ryder's post-cutting crew up-river; town visitors.

articles.text:
LITTLE MISSOURI, FEB. 24, 1884.

EDITOR COW BOY:

In your last issue some pilgrim who signs his name “How” had a lot of stuff about the old times in Little Missouri. He gives himself dead away. It was Frank Moore who nearly killed the drunken butcher, when the fight occurred in the back room. I was there and know about that. So does Paddock, Henry Hudson and lots of the other folks who were here then.

There never was such a man as “Bloody Hand” here. The party referred to was called “Stug” or “Guitar Strings” or some such name. I know for I was there and knew all the parties well.

“How” had better dry up on things he don't know anything about.

Will write soon again.

POST T. RADER.
articles.summary: Letter signed “Post T. Rader” disputing “How's” account of Little Missouri's early days: Frank Moore nearly killed a drunken butcher in a back-room fight.

articles.text:
LITTLE MISSOURI, Feb. 26.

EDITOR COW BOY:

In your paper of last week, I noticed a line about the buffalo shot here and a request for some hump and tender steaks. I would be a mighty mean man to impose on a “tenderfoot,” who wore a four-dollar set of store teeth, by sending him a steak that would “bust his gums” as well as his teeth. Wait until you become a “tough” and hold the garden claim, old boy, then I'll fire hump at you for a week right along. It's better to do so than to ring in any veteran of the herd on you now. If you got outside ten or twelve pounds of that steak you would pass in your chips, and some vandal would plant a tent and stake (steak) a claim on your grave.

Sadly yours,

HOWARD EATON.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton's joking reply to the editor's request for buffalo hump steak.
